concepts.name: Timed background work without overlapping runs (PeriodicTimer vs Timer)
OpenTelemetry Baggage: propagation, attributes and risks
Breaking changes and choosing an API versioning scheme

questions.prompt: A `BackgroundService` must run `SyncAsync()` every 30 seconds, but one run can take 45 seconds, and runs must never overlap. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A `System.Threading.Timer` whose callback starts `SyncAsync()` on each 30-second tick
A `PeriodicTimer` loop that starts each tick's `SyncAsync()` with `Task.Run`, unawaited
A `PeriodicTimer` loop: `while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(ct)) await SyncAsync();`
A `Timer` callback that calls `SyncAsync()` and counts active runs with `Interlocked.Increment`

questions.explanation: A `Timer` doesn't wait for the previous callback to finish, so a 45-second run overlaps the next tick; counting runs with `Interlocked` doesn't stop that. Awaiting the work inside a `PeriodicTimer` loop means the next wait only starts after the run ends, and ticks missed meanwhile are coalesced into one, so runs never overlap. Firing the work off with `Task.Run` brings the overlap back.

sources.title: Background tasks with hosted services in ASP.NET Core
sources.claim: System.Threading.Timer doesn't wait for previous executions of DoWork to finish; the asynchronous timed background task example awaits DoWork inside a while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken)) loop with a PeriodicTimer.

sources.title: PeriodicTimer.WaitForNextTickAsync(CancellationToken) Method
sources.claim: PeriodicTimer behaves like an auto-reset event: multiple ticks are coalesced into one if they occur between calls to WaitForNextTickAsync, which may only be used by one consumer at a time.

questions.prompt: Service A puts `customer.id` into OpenTelemetry Baggage, then calls Service B over HTTP. Service B wants that value on its own spans. What must B do?

choices.text: Nothing, since Baggage entries become attributes on every span by default
Read the value from Baggage and add it to its spans as an attribute
Nothing, since Service A's span attributes are copied onto Service B's span
Look up Service A's trace in the backend and join it on the shared trace ID

questions.explanation: Baggage is a key-value store that propagates with the context (in HTTP headers), but it is separate from span, metric and log attributes: nothing copies it onto telemetry unless your code reads it and adds it. Span attributes don't propagate between services at all.

sources.title: Baggage
sources.claim: Baggage is a separate key-value store propagated alongside context in HTTP headers, and it is not associated with attributes on spans, metrics or logs unless you explicitly read it and add it.

questions.prompt: Your public REST API must change `address` from a string into an object, and partner apps you don't control depend on it. How do you ship the change, and how do you choose where the version goes?

model_answer.summary: Restructuring a field breaks existing clients, so ship it as a new version and keep the old one working. Choose URI, query string, header or media type versioning by their trade-offs, such as caching and simplicity.
key_points: Adding a field that clients can ignore usually isn't breaking, but restructuring, renaming or removing a field like `address` is
Expose the new shape as a new version, and keep the existing version returning the original schema for current clients
URI (`/v2/...`) and query string versioning are simple and cache-friendly; header and media type versioning keep one URI per resource but need more request logic and can duplicate data in caches
Default to a meaningful version, such as 1, when a client doesn't send one

questions.explanation: Versioning lets you change the API without breaking clients you don't control. The tempting answer is to change the field in place and tell partners, but anyone who parses `address` as a string breaks the moment you deploy. Each placement of the version has costs, so the choice is a trade-off rather than one right answer.

sources.title: Web API Design Best Practices - Azure Architecture Center
sources.claim: Adding fields clients can ignore might not be breaking, but removing or renaming fields or restructuring resources can be; URI, query string, header and media type versioning keep existing versions working, URI and query string versioning are cache-friendly, header and media type versioning need more logic and can duplicate cached data, and an omitted version should default to a meaningful value like 1.

questions.prompt: A loop awaits `WaitForNextTickAsync` on a 30-second `PeriodicTimer`, and one run of the work takes 100 seconds. What happens when that run ends?

choices.text: The next wait completes at once, for one tick; the missed ticks coalesce
Three queued ticks complete one after another, so the work runs three times
The timer has stopped, because ticks fired while no wait was in flight
It waits a full 30 seconds from the end of the run before the next tick

questions.explanation: `PeriodicTimer` behaves like an auto-reset event: ticks that fire between calls to `WaitForNextTickAsync` are coalesced into one. So the three ticks missed during the 100-second run become a single pending tick, the next wait returns immediately, and the loop then follows the timer's schedule again. The timer keeps running until it is disposed.

sources.title: PeriodicTimer.WaitForNextTickAsync(CancellationToken) Method
sources.claim: PeriodicTimer behaves like an auto-reset event, in that multiple ticks are coalesced into a single tick if they occur between calls to WaitForNextTickAsync; it returns false when the timer is disposed.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't you put a user's email address into OpenTelemetry Baggage?

choices.text: Baggage can only hold numeric values, so strings such as email addresses are dropped
Baggage is saved with every span in the backend, so it fills trace storage quickly
Baggage is encrypted with a key per service, so downstream services can't read it
It travels in HTTP headers and can reach unintended services, like third-party APIs

questions.explanation: Baggage is propagated in HTTP headers, and automatic instrumentation sends it on outgoing requests, so it can reach services you didn't mean to share it with, including third-party APIs. There are also no built-in integrity checks. It isn't stored on spans unless you add it, and it isn't encrypted.

sources.title: Baggage
sources.claim: Baggage and trace context are sent in HTTP headers, baggage items can be shared with unintended resources such as third-party APIs because instrumentation includes them in network requests, and there are no built-in integrity checks.

questions.prompt: Which change to a JSON response can existing clients usually absorb without a new API version?

choices.text: Adding a `dateCreated` field that older clients can just ignore
Renaming the `name` field to `displayName` to match the new UI
Turning `address` from a string into an object with a `city` key
Removing the `fax` field, since analytics show nobody reads it

questions.explanation: Clients that ignore fields they don't recognise keep working when a field is added. Renaming, restructuring or removing a field can break any client that reads it, and usage analytics can't prove that no client depends on it, so those changes call for a new version.

sources.title: Web API Design Best Practices - Azure Architecture Center
sources.claim: Adding content to existing resources might not be a breaking change because clients that don't expect it ignore it, while field removals, renaming or restructuring can constitute breaking changes that need a versioning approach.
